text:
Kang and McAuley’s [SASRec (2018)](https://arxiv.org/html/1808.09781v1) compares against first-order MC, FPMC and order-insensitive FISM. Petrov et al.’s [Do Sequential Recommendation Benchmarks Require Higher-Order Sequence Modelling? (2026)](https://research.atspotify.com/2026/10/do-sequential-recommendation-benchmarks-require-higher-order-sequence-modelling) provides a closer mechanism comparison: last-item MC/FMC/FMC+, recency-weighted Sequential Rules/PCTM, and SASRec/eSASRec under shared splits. Pairwise history models beat both Transformers on three Amazon datasets; these are different categories from this task. Neither study establishes the exact exponentially decayed embedding-pooling control; include that separately, alongside uniform pooling and last-item scoring, with matched embeddings, loss and tuning effort.

[Sequence or Pseudo-Sequence? (2021)](https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-2955/paper8.pdf) shuffled training histories while retaining validation/test targets; SASRec often changed little, highlighting ambiguous timestamps and weak evidence for chronological dependence. Suggested diagnostics here: shuffle older history while preserving the last item; shuffle the recent window; retain only the last k items; remove recent versus equally many older items; replace recent items with training-popularity-matched items. Preserve splits, labels, candidates and evaluation seeds. Separate inference perturbations, which measure sensitivity, from retrained controls, which test whether order adds learnable value; removing positional embeddings alone does not eliminate causal-mask order information.

Define per-category slices using training-only counts and thresholds: target-popularity head/middle/tail, short/medium/long training histories, and mean history popularity; cross popularity with history length. Report paired validation HR@10 changes, slice sizes and uncertainty, retaining four-category macro HR@10 for selection. Gains beyond last-item and decayed pooling, surviving popularity matching and appearing across slices, support useful history dependence; gains concentrated in popular targets or active users suggest shortcuts, without proving causality.
